OMIM:613721.summary_plain: Epileptic encephalopathy, early infantile, 11 is linked to SCN2A changes. Research papers show SCN2A changes can make the sodium channel work too much, and some changes may also make it work too little or in mixed ways. This condition is also being studied in several research studies.

steps.text: Research records show SCN2A causes this condition. [E00026]
One paper says some SCN2A changes may make the sodium channel work more. [Mfce5014c]
Another paper says one SCN2A change may act in mixed ways, with both less and more channel work. [M30b5f5fe, Md58c8bdc]
Several studies are listed for this condition, including an SCN2A study and a broad epilepsy study. [T00052, T00053, T00054, T00058]
This condition is also being compared with related epilepsy conditions, but those similarities are only hypotheses. [E00228, E00229, S00001]

uncertainties: The records do not show which exact SCN2A change your family has.
One paper is from lab studies, so it may not match every child with this condition.
The study records say SCN2A in the title or keywords, but some notes say this should be checked.
This atlas does not track treatments. Ask your care team about current treatment options.

next_step.text: Ask a doctor who knows genes to review the exact SCN2A change together with the study listings. [E00026, T00052, T00053, T00054, T00058]

OMIM:614558.summary_plain: Epileptic encephalopathy, early infantile, 13 is linked to changes in SCN8A. Research papers show those changes can make the sodium channel work too much. That can raise brain cell firing and help trigger seizures.

steps.text: We found a direct link between SCN8A and this condition. That link is well supported in curated records.
Research papers show SCN8A changes may make the sodium channel work more. One paper says patient-derived changes have gain-of-function effects.
Another paper says a recurring SCN8A change can impair channel inactivation. That is consistent with brain cells firing too easily and seizures.
Records also show this condition is being studied in SCN8A-focused studies. Those include NBI-921352, PRAX-562, and two study records tied to SCN8A-DEE.
There is also a study shared with Epileptic encephalopathy, early infantile, 11. That shared study does not prove the same cause, but it suggests related care research.

uncertainties: Some study records say to confirm the exact disease or change in scope. That means fit for your family may need expert review.
The gain-of-function message is supported by cited papers, but the papers mention different changes and contexts.
Some links, like shared mechanism or phenotype similarity, are only hypotheses. They should not be treated as proven shared biology.
I do not see detailed age, seizure type, or variant-specific guidance for every child in these records.

next_step.text: Ask a doctor who knows genes to review the SCN8A papers and the study records together. Focus on the cited SCN8A gain-of-function reports and the SCN8A-DEE study records.

OMIM:613720.summary_plain: KCNQ2 changes are linked to Epileptic encephalopathy, early infantile, 7. This condition is tied to both loss- and gain-of-function changes in KCNQ2, but those are linked to different reports. Several studies and patient resources also exist for KCNQ2-related epilepsy.

steps.text: Research papers show KCNQ2 causes this condition. That link is well supported.
Some reports say KCNQ2 changes can make the potassium channel work less. That is one known pattern in this condition.
Other reports say KCNQ2 changes can make the potassium channel work more. Those reports are also tied to this condition.
Records show studies for this condition, including a KCNQ2 patient register, a study of XEN496, and an omics study. These can help families and doctors learn more.

uncertainties: The gain-of-function and loss-of-function reports are not one single shared rule. They may reflect different changes, symptoms, or patient groups.
The study records say KCNQ2 is in the title or keywords, but some notes say the exact fit should be confirmed.
We do not have full trial results here, so we cannot say how well any study worked.
The similar-disease links are only guesses, not proof of the same cause.

next_step.text: Ask a doctor who knows genes to review the KCNQ2 reports and the study records together, especially the loss-of-function and gain-of-function papers.

OMIM:614959.summary_plain: Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 14 is strongly linked to KCNT1 changes. Research papers show many KCNT1 changes make this potassium channel work more. That helps explain why this condition can cause severe seizures and brain development problems. We also found active KCNT1 studies and a registry.

steps.text: Research papers show KCNT1 causes Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 14. This link is well supported.
Several papers say many KCNT1 changes make the potassium channel work more. That is a gain of function effect.
That change may help explain the severe seizure problems seen in this condition. The papers describe abnormal nerve cell excitability.
Records show ongoing KCNT1 studies and a KCNT1 patient registry. These may help families learn about research updates.

uncertainties: We do not have proof from these records that every KCNT1 change acts the same way.
The study records name KCNT1 in titles, but they ask for expert confirmation of fit.
The records do not show which children match which study, or who can join.
The similarity links to other epileptic encephalopathies are only hints, not proof of shared cause.

next_step.text: Ask a doctor who knows genes to review the KCNT1 gain-of-function papers and the KCNT1 registry together. Use the cited studies and registry to check whether any family member’s change matches the research papers.

OMIM:615473.summary_plain: Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 17 is linked to changes in GNAO1. Research papers also suggest some changes may make GNAO1 signaling work too strongly, while one mouse study describes a severe change that blocks normal turning off of the signal. A few studies and support resources are already listed for this condition.

steps.text: Research records show GNAO1 causes this condition. The link is strongly supported.
Some animal studies suggest certain GNAO1 changes may make G protein signaling work too much. These include G203R and G184S.
Another animal study describes G203R as a severe dominant negative change. That means it may interfere with the normal protein’s job, but this needs expert review because the study is in animals.

Research records also list several studies for this condition, including a GNAO1 natural history study and other GNAO1-focused studies. These may help families and doctors follow what is being studied now.

uncertainties: The exact change-to-change pattern is not settled. One animal record suggests gain of function, while another suggests dominant negative action for G203R.
The study records named here do not prove the exact patient group in scope. Several notes say the condition or change should be confirmed.
The listed studies are about study and follow-up, not proven benefit.
This atlas does not track treatments. Ask your care team about current treatment options.

next_step.text: Ask a doctor who knows genes to review the GNAO1 change with the cited animal findings and the listed GNAO1 study records.

OMIM:607745.summary_plain: Seizures, benign familial infantile, 3 is linked to SCN2A. Research papers also suggest some SCN2A changes make the sodium channel work less. That fits a possible loss-of-function pattern in this condition.

steps.text: Research records show SCN2A can cause Seizures, benign familial infantile, 3. That is the clearest link we found. [E00175]
One published study says an SCN2A change, S863F, reduced current density. This suggests a loss-of-function change, meaning the channel may work less well. [M13d4d49b]
There is also a second SCN2A-related seizure condition in the records. That means related seizure types may overlap, but this is not proof of the same cause or treatment response. [E00252,E00026]
The records also list the FamilieSCN2A Foundation as serving people with this condition. That may be a useful support contact. [C00004]

uncertainties: The loss-of-function idea comes from one cited study and one change only. It may not apply to every SCN2A change in this condition.
We did not find a study record named specifically for Seizures, benign familial infantile, 3.
The two trial records in the input are for SCN2A-DEE, not this exact condition. They may not match your group’s needs.

next_step.text: Ask a doctor who knows genes to review the SCN2A S863F finding and the exact diagnosis match. If useful, also contact the FamilieSCN2A Foundation for patient-facing support. [M13d4d49b,C00004]

OMIM:617080.summary_plain: Seizures, benign familial infantile, 5 is linked to SCN8A. Research papers show one SCN8A change may make the sodium channel work more, which could help explain this condition.

steps.text: Records show SCN8A causes Seizures, benign familial infantile, 5. This is the main known link for this condition.
Research papers show one SCN8A change may make the sodium channel work more. In plain words, the channel may stay too active and make brain cells fire too much.
We also found a similar seizure condition linked to SCN8A, but that match is only a guess. It does not prove the same cause or same change here.
Support groups are listed for this condition, so families may have a place to ask questions and find community help.

uncertainties: We only found one direct cause link for this condition, so the full range of SCN8A changes is not shown here.
The SCN8A change evidence is about one reported case, so it may not apply to every child.
The similar-condition match is only a hypothesis, not proof of shared biology.
We did not find a direct study or patient list for Seizures, benign familial infantile, 5 in the records here.

next_step.text: Ask a doctor who knows genes to review the SCN8A finding and the quoted study note, and ask whether any family testing would be useful.
